title: An AI system is not just a single model
body: An AI system isn’t made up of just a single model.
when_to_show: AI Services, RAG, and Agent Issues
detail: Actual services involve multiple stages, such as input preparation, searching, evidence selection, prompt generation, model invocation, output validation, log storage, and cost management. The model is merely the core component responsible for generating answers or making decisions. When reading code, don’t just look at the line that calls the model; to understand the overall structure, you must also examine what data is prepared beforehand and what validation is performed afterward.

title: Prompt: Instructions for the model
body: A prompt is a set of instructions given to the model.
when_to_show: When reviewing prompt, llm, instruction, output_format
detail: While it can consist solely of a user’s question, in actual services, it often includes the model’s role, response format, prohibited actions, reference materials, and examples. A good prompt clearly tells the model what it should and should not do. When reading code, if the prompt is a long string, it should be treated as a critical setting for adjusting output quality.

title: Context Window: The range the model can see at one time
body: A context window is the amount of information a model can reference in one request. The limit is measured in tokens rather than characters, and system instructions, the user request, prior conversation, and retrieved documents all share that space. If the input is too large, an API may reject it or the application may need to remove content, leaving less room for the answer.
when_to_show: Chunks, RAG, and the Challenge of Processing Long Documents
detail: The context window is the maximum amount of input a model can process at one time. Since it cannot accommodate entire long documents or lengthy conversations, it is necessary to perform searches, summarization, chunk selection, and prioritization. When reading code, ensure that the prompt length, the number of search results, and the maximum token setting do not conflict with one another.

title: Chunking: Breaking Down Long Documents
body: Chunking is the process of dividing a long document into smaller pieces. Since models and search systems have difficulty handling documents that are too long all at once, they split them into paragraphs or sections and store and search them in that format. In RAG, chunks relevant to the query are identified and passed to the model.
when_to_show: JSONL, RAG, and Document Processing Problems
detail: Chunking is the process of dividing a long document into searchable units. If the chunks are too large, irrelevant content may be included; if they are too small, necessary context may be lost. When reading the code, you must examine the chunk size, overlap, metadata on the original text’s location, and whether the title is preserved to understand the search quality.

title: Fine-tuning: Changing the Model's Behavior
body: Fine-tuning uses additional training data to adapt output format, tone, decision patterns, or task ability. It may teach some facts, but it is not a guaranteed way to retrieve current knowledge; changing facts are better handled with retrieval or tools. Check the train/evaluation split, base model, checkpoint, and model actually loaded for inference.
when_to_show: Training Data, LoRA, and Model Improvement Issues

title: LoRA: How to Perform Lightweight Fine-Tuning
body: LoRA is a method for tailoring a large model to a specific format or task by training only a small set of additional weights, without having to retrain the entire model. Training the entire model is costly and time-consuming, but LoRA allows for relatively lightweight experimentation. However, LoRA does not provide all the necessary knowledge from scratch, so data quality and the target format are crucial.
when_to_show: When reviewing lora, finetuning, adapter, gpu
detail: It’s easier to understand LoRA as a method that involves training the model with small adapter weights rather than modifying the entire large model directly. In the code, the base model path and the adapter path are often defined separately. Checking whether the adapter is used separately or combined with the base model during inference can help you better understand the execution structure.

title: Inference: The step of generating answers using the trained model
body: Inference is the process of using a trained model to generate actual answers or predictions.
when_to_show: Issues with model calls, APIs, and server costs
detail: If training is the process of teaching the model, then inference is the process of feeding input into the trained model and receiving the results. When a chatbot answers a question or an image model classifies an image, that is also inference. When reading code, inference involves model loading, input preprocessing, prediction execution, and output postprocessing.

title: Latency: The time it takes to receive a response
body: Latency is the time it takes for a response to be returned after a request is sent. In AI apps, model calls, searches, database queries, and network round-trip times all affect latency. If the response takes too long, users may feel as though the service has stopped working.
when_to_show: When reviewing latency, performance, api, rag
detail: Latency is directly linked to the wait time experienced by the user. In AI apps, searches, database queries, model calls, post-processing, and network round trips all contribute to latency. When reviewing the code, it’s easy to identify bottlenecks by checking for repetitive calls, caching, timeouts, and streaming processing.

title: Hallucination: A Plausible Wrong Answer
body: Hallucination is fluent output that is unsupported or false. Retrieval, citations, validators, and abstention rules can reduce risk but do not guarantee accuracy. Verify that citations support the claims and use trusted tools or rules for consequential facts.
when_to_show: When reviewing hallucination, rag, evidence, evaluation

title: Guardrail: A Safety Mechanism for AI Outputs
body: Guardrail is a safety mechanism for AI outputs. Since models can generate incorrect, dangerous, or unformatted answers, services implement safeguards such as prohibition rules, output validation, justification checks, and handling of follow-up questions. For example, in a learning app, rules can be set to restrict terminology that exceeds a student’s level or to provide hints rather than immediately revealing the correct answer.
when_to_show: When reviewing guardrail, safety, policy, validation
detail: A guardrail is a safety mechanism applied before and after model output. It may include rules such as blocking prohibited topics, removing personal information, limiting the model to student-level responses, validating the output format, and withholding answers when there is insufficient evidence. When reading the code, distinguish whether the guardrail filters the input before the model is called or checks the results after the call.
